Abstract
Disaggregated memory (DM) is a promising data center archi-
tecture that decouples CPU and memory into independent re-
source pools to improve resource utilization. Building on DM,
memory-disaggregated key-value (KV) stores are adopted to
efficiently manage remote data. Unfortunately, existing ap-
proaches suffer from poor performance due to two critical
issues: 1) the overdependence on one-sided atomic opera-
tions in index processing, and 2) the constrained efficiency
in compute-side caches. To address these issues, we propose
FlexKV, a memory-disaggregated KV store with index proxy-
ing. Our key idea is to dynamically offload the index to com-
pute nodes, leveraging their powerful CPUs to accelerate in-
dex processing and maintain high-performance compute-side
caches. Three challenges have to be addressed to enable effi-
cient index proxying on DM, i.e., the load imbalance across
compute nodes, the limited memory of compute nodes, and
the expensive cache coherence overhead. FlexKV proposes:
1) a rank-aware hotness detection algorithm to continuously
balance index load across compute nodes, 2) a two-level CN
memory optimization scheme to efficiently utilize compute
node memory, and 3) an RPC-aggregated cache management
mechanism to reduce cache coherence overhead. The experi
mental results show that FlexKV improves throughput by up
to 2.94× and reduces latency by up to 85.2%, compared with
the state-of-the-art memory-disaggregated KV stores.
1 Introduction
Disaggregated memory (DM), a promising data center archi
tecture proposed to improve resource efficiency, has gained
significant attention from both industry [6, 35, 67, 79, 80]
and academia [18, 39, 40, 60]. DM breaks the boundaries of
monolithic servers by decoupling CPUs and memory into the
compute pool (compute nodes, CNs) and the memory pool
(memory nodes, MNs), connected via high-performance net-
works like RDMA [28, 54] and CXL [10, 36, 85, 86]. This
architecture enables CPUs and memory to be flexibly allo
cated, enhancing overall resource efficiency.
Key-value (KV) stores are emerging applications on
DM [25, 33, 51, 62, 65]. Scalability, i.e., the ability to serve
more clients without significant performance degradation, is
a key requirement for all memory-disaggregated KV stores.
However, existing approaches still struggle to achieve this
goal due to the following two primary issues.
The overdependence on one-sided atomic operations in
index processing. Existing memory-disaggregated KV stores
extensively rely on one-sided atomic operations (i.e., CAS and
FAA) to resolve concurrency conflicts during index process-
ing [88]. Unfortunately, the extensive number of one-sided
atomic operations generates a severe performance bottleneck
on DMs implemented with both RDMA and CXL. Specif-
ically, for RDMA-based DM, atomic operations with more
complex semantics consume more processing power than
read or write operations [31], making the processing units of
RDMA network interface cards (RNICs) a bottleneck. Mean-
while, for CXL-based DM, atomic operations hinder system
performance due to the expensive cross-node cache coherence
protocol (i.e., CXL.cache in CXL 3.0) [10, 41, 48, 63].
The constrained efficiency in compute-side caches. Due
to the significant performance gap between remote and lo-
cal memory, using the local memory of CNs as caches is
a common practice in many memory-disaggregated KV
stores [33, 42, 46]. To reduce cross-node cache coherence
overhead, existing designs either cache only the index (i.e.,
addresses of KV pairs) [45,62,65] or cache both the index and
KV pairs but partition the ownership of cached data to individ-
ual CNs [33,42]. However, both approaches are suboptimal in
terms of system performance. The former requires at least one
remote memory access per request even on cache hits, while
the latter introduces additional overhead from forwarding KV
requests to designated nodes that own the requested data.
In this paper, we propose to offload part of the index to
the compute pool to address the above issues simultaneously.

processing, converting expensive one-sided atomic operations
into local CPU operations. Furthermore, during the offloaded
index processing, CNs can efficiently cache KV pairs, enhanc-
ing compute-side cache efficiency. However, three challenges
have to be addressed to achieve this idea in practice.

partitions may experience vastly different access frequencies

with static assignment, hot partitions can overload certain

performance. Moreover, workload patterns are dynamic in
production environments [7, 27, 37, 78], requiring continuous

pute nodes (CNs) and memory nodes (MNs). CNs have ample
CPUs but limited memory, while MNs have abundant mem-

flexible, on-demand allocation of CPU and memory resources

tional sockets, requiring CPU participation at both ends.

Based on the design of compute-side caches, existing ap-
proaches can also be classified into two categories.
(1) Address-only cache. To minimize the overhead of main-

the index (i.e., addresses of KV pairs), as shown in Figure 2(a).

the ownership of data among CNs, where each CN handles

one CN updates data. However, they adopt a client-CN-MN

Existing memory-disaggregated KV stores typically rely on
one-sided atomic operations to resolve concurrency conflicts.
As mentioned in §1, these one-sided atomic operations are
more complex and incur greater overhead on the processing
units within RNICs. In these KV stores, frequent invoca-
tion of one-sided atomic operations can easily make the MN

CPUs handle concurrency conflicts using two-sided RPCs
(RDMA_SEND&RECV) together with local atomic instructions
(LOCAL_CAS) can significantly improve performance, as they
are more lightweight and avoid accessing the MNs.

4.3 Two-Level CN Memory Optimization
In the DM architecture, CNs have abundant CPUs but very
limited memory. A CN typically has only about 10% of the
memory of a single MN [42, 65, 81], or even less [33, 45, 71].
Index proxying offloads part of the index from MNs to CNs
increases pressure on the already limited CN memory and can
even degrade performance (Challenge 2).
To address this challenge, FlexKV employs the two-level CN
memory optimization scheme. At the first level, slot-resolved
index RPCs are used to reduce the inherent space overhead
of the local index. At the second level, an adaptive index
cache splitting technique is applied to efficiently partition CN
memory between the local index and local cache.
4.3.1 Slot-Resolved Index RPC
In many DM index designs, the index alone cannot pinpoint a
key’s exact index slot without reading the corresponding KV
pair. For example, SMART [46] and RACE [89] store only
partial keys or fingerprints, so a key identifies only candidate
index slots. The system must fetch the KV pairs referenced
by those slots from MNs to confirm the correct one before
performing updates. Consequently, in FlexKV, a proxy cannot
resolve a key’s index slot from the key when serving index
RPCs. An alternative is to maintain a direct mapping from
keys to slot addresses within the CN’s local index, but this
map requires storing keys. With variable-sized keys (e.g.,
strings), the memory overhead becomes substantial, making
the local index prohibitively memory-intensive.
To make the local index lightweight, FlexKV issues slot-
resolved RPCs. This design is enabled by the fact that, for fault
tolerance, the proxy synchronizes every local index update to
the MNs’ index (§4.5). This allows clients to resolve a key’s
index slot address at the MNs before sending index RPCs
to the proxy, thereby avoiding the proxy’s own slot lookup
and the memory-intensive key-to-slot map. Furthermore, to
reduce index lookup traffic to MNs, FlexKV employs different
index-resolution strategies for write and read requests.
Slot-Resolved Write Requests. For write requests (i.e.,
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), FlexKV has clients resolve the tar-
get index slot before issuing index RPCs to the proxy,
as shown in Figure 7. Specifically, the client RDMA_READs
the MNs’ index by key to find candidate index slots (❶),
RDMA_READs the referenced KV pairs to confirm the correct
one (❷), and then sends that slot address along with the RPC
(❸). The proxy can then update the designated slot directly
without a key-based lookup. Notably, this approach does not
add client-side burden and maintains correctness because it
follows the original one-sided index protocol exactly, except
for replacing the client’s RDMA_CAS with a LOCAL_CAS at the
proxy, while other procedures remain identical. To acceler-
ate slot resolution, FlexKV embeds the slot address in each
key’s cache entry (i.e., the KV pair or its address), so the full
resolution path is taken only when the local cache misses.
Fast-Path Read Requests. For read requests (i.e., SEARCH),
clients bypass slot resolution and issue index RPCs directly,
with the proxy returning all candidate index slots based on the
key (①). The client then fetches the KV pairs from these slots
and finds the one whose key matches (②). Since slot collisions
are rare, the proxy typically returns only one candidate slot.
With this design, most read requests are efficiently served by
the proxy, reducing index lookup traffic to MNs.
4.3.2 Adaptive Index-Cache Splitting
Once the local index is introduced on CNs, CN memory must
be shared between the local index and the local cache. Under
tight CN memory budgets, allocating memory between these
two components is challenging. Overprovisioning one compo-
nent can starve the other, sometimes leading to performance
even worse than a simpler design that only has the local cache.
Moreover, the optimal memory split is workload-dependent
and time-varying (e.g., skew shifts, read-write ratio changes),
making static partitioning inherently suboptimal.
To address this issue, FlexKV employs an adaptive index-
cache splitting technique to search for a near-optimal memory
split under dynamic workloads. Specifically, it 1) introduces
a unified index-offload ratio across all CNs to reduce the
search space, and 2) applies a throughput-guided knob that
dynamically tunes this ratio in response to workload shifts.
Unified Index-Offload Ratio. FlexKV uses a sampling-based
approach that adjusts the memory split based on observed
throughput, offering robustness and implementation simplic-
ity. However, a naive sampler can be slow to converge due

ratio between offloaded partitions and total partitions in the

same ratio to determine the memory allocated to their local
index, with the remaining memory assigned to the local cache.

similar access frequencies (§4.2), applying this cluster-wide
index-offload ratio naturally balances the load.

To make the local index lightweight, FlexKV issues slot-

4.3.2 Adaptive Index-Cache Splitting
Once the local index is introduced on CNs, CN memory must
be shared between the local index and the local cache. Under
tight CN memory budgets, allocating memory between these
two components is challenging. Overprovisioning one compo-
nent can starve the other, sometimes leading to performance
even worse than a simpler design that only has the local cache.
Moreover, the optimal memory split is workload-dependent
and time-varying (e.g., skew shifts, read-write ratio changes),
making static partitioning inherently suboptimal.
To address this issue, FlexKV employs an adaptive index-
cache splitting technique to search for a near-optimal memory
split under dynamic workloads. Specifically, it 1) introduces
a unified index-offload ratio across all CNs to reduce the
search space, and 2) applies a throughput-guided knob that
dynamically tunes this ratio in response to workload shifts.
Unified Index-Offload Ratio. FlexKV uses a sampling-based
approach that adjusts the memory split based on observed
throughput, offering robustness and implementation simplic-

to the large search space: with C CNs, there are C split vari-

FlexKV introduces a unified index-offload ratio, defined as the
ratio between offloaded partitions and total partitions in the
per-CN hot-to-cold partition list (Figure 6). All CNs use the
same ratio to determine the memory allocated to their local
index, with the remaining memory assigned to the local cache.
Since index partitions at the same rank across CNs exhibit
similar access frequencies (§4.2), applying this cluster-wide
index-offload ratio naturally balances the load.

4.5 Put It All Together
This section presents the complete framework of FlexKV, in-
tegrating the three previously presented design components.
Index Structure. Without loss of generality, following exist-
ing studies [25, 62, 65, 83, 84], we use a hash table [89] as a
case study for indexing KV pairs. The hashtable is divided
into subtables, which serve as the granularity for index parti-
tioning among proxies in our implementation. Each subtable
contains contiguous buckets, each consisting of contiguous
8-byte slots. A slot comprises a 48-bit address field for the
KV pair’s location in the memory pool, an 8-bit length field
for the KV pair size, and an 8-bit fingerprint field for prelim-
inary key matching during lookups. The index uses 8-byte
CAS operations to atomically modify index slots.
Memory Management. To ensure high read performance [25,
62, 65, 89], the out-of-place update scheme is employed for
KV pairs, where each write request allocates a new KV pair
before modifying the index. To manage KV pair space, FlexKV
employs a two-level method [25, 62]. Clients first request
coarse-grained memory blocks (e.g., 16 MB) from MNs when
their free space is insufficient, then allocate fine-grained KV
pairs from these blocks upon receiving write requests.
Workflows. Figure 10 presents the FlexKV workflows through
which clients execute the four types of KV requests: INSERT,
UPDATE, SEARCH, and DELETE. As FlexKV’s design mainly tar-
gets proxy-managed index partitions, we concentrate on these

follow identical protocols to existing one-sided RDMA based
KV stores [25, 62], and are omitted for brevity.
(1) Write. For a write request (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE),
the client first writes the new KV pair to MNs while resolving
the index slot address. The resolution can be skipped when
the local cache is hit (§4.3.1). After this, the client issues
an index RPC to the proxy, which then invalidates previous
caches: (i) for cached addresses, the proxy clears the previ-
ously committed KV pair’s valid bit to invalidate (§2.2.2);
(ii) for cached KV pairs, the proxy sends RPCs to those CNs
on the sharer list to invalidate (§4.4). In parallel, the proxy
writes the new index slot to the MNs’ index for fault toler-

LOCAL_CAS (commit point) and replies to the client.

the local cache. If a cached KV pair exists, the client immedi-
ately returns the result. If a cached address exists, the client
performs an RDMA_READ to fetch the KV pair from MNs and
verifies the match. If both miss, the client sends an index RPC
to the proxy to obtain the address of the latest committed KV
pair (§4.3.1), which is then retrieved via RDMA_READ.

uses a local key-to-lock map to ensure only one write request
per key is processed at a time. Concurrent writes to keys
already in process will fail immediately, as in CAS. Since
in-flight RPCs are few, the map size remains negligible.

no Byzantine failures [24] occur, following previous work [25,
51, 62, 83]. (1) For the manager, it only performs periodic

Impact of Proxy Thread Number. In FlexKV, each proxy
runs multiple threads to process index RPCs concurrently.
Figure 20 shows throughput under YCSB workloads with dif-
ferent numbers of proxy threads. Throughput first increases
with the number of threads, peaks at 2 threads, and then de
clines due to resource contention (e.g., lock contention on
multithreaded data structures and RNIC cache thrashing from

threads to 2. Considering CNs’ abundant CPUs and FlexKV’s
up to 2.94× performance improvement, this modest 20% ex-

already achieves 71.8–90.2% of the peak throughput, indicat-

128B steps. As the KV size grows, throughput of all systems
gradually decreases and their performance gap narrows due
to bandwidth saturation. Nevertheless, FlexKV consistently
achieves the highest throughput among the four systems.

only 3 MNs, here we vary the CN-MN ratio from 3:20 to
10:13 to evaluate FlexKV’s scalability, as shown in Figure 22.

which mitigate the MN-side network bottleneck. The subse
quent decrease occurs because each client reaches its CPU
limit, and fewer CNs reduce the total number of clients. For
Clover, performance remains limited by the metadata server,
so varying CN-MN ratios has little effect.

6 Related Work
Disaggregated Memory. Existing studies on DM include
software-based approaches, such as modifying operating sys-
for seamless integration, as well as efforts to optimize data
structures [14, 45, 59, 71, 85, 87] and specific applications like
in-memory KV stores [1, 25, 33, 42, 51, 62] and transactional
storage systems [44, 74, 83, 84]. On the other hand, hardware-
based approaches [36, 39, 50, 63] and hardware-software co-
designed methods [22, 34, 72] are being explored to enhance
functionality. FlexKV, an advanced KV store designed for DM,
can also benefit from these low-level optimizations.
Memory-Disaggregated KV Stores. Recently, many KV
stores targeting DM architectures have emerged, such as
Clover [65], FUSEE [62], DINOMO [33], Aceso [25], and
SWARM-KV [51], each with its unique design focus: Clover
reduces monetary and energy costs, FUSEE disaggregates
metadata management, DINOMO leverages ownership par
titioning for cache efficiency, Aceso uses erasure coding to
save space, and SWARM-KV trades space for one-RTT oper
ations. Finally, FlexKV focuses on scalable index processing
and flexible KV pair caching to improve performance.
Memory-Disaggregated Index Processing. In memory
disaggregated KV stores, index processing are handled in
various ways. Clover [65] relies on monolithic metadata
servers, which limits resource efficiency and can become
the performance bottleneck. Aceso [25] and FUSEE [62]
let CN CPUs manage the index in MNs remotely via one-
sided RDMA. DEX [42] also uses one-sided RDMA but can
offload some operations to MN CPUs for local execution,
requiring MN compute power. DINOMO [33] relies entirely
on MN CPUs, demanding significant MN compute power. In
contrast, FlexKV allows CN CPUs to either manage the index
remotely via one-sided RDMA or act as the proxies for local
execution, without imposing any compute overhead on MNs.
Memory-Disaggregated Caching. Ditto [61] is a memory
disaggregated caching system for backup storage. It stores
cached data in MNs and performs distributed eviction via
one-sided RDMA. In contrast, FlexKV stores cached data in
CNs and performs local eviction via CN CPUs. DiFache [82],
a concurrent work with FlexKV, is a general-purpose caching
system for DM applications. It stores cached data in CNs but
keeps cache directory in MNs, which is managed via one-
sided RDMA. In contrast, FlexKV stores both cached data and
cache directory in CNs, and directory management is piggy-
backed on index RPCs, reducing extra network overhead.
7 Conclusion
This paper presents FlexKV, a memory-disaggregated KV
store with index proxying. FlexKV offloads the index to CNs
dynamically and introduces KV pair caching across CNs,
addressing the bottleneck at MN RNICs. Evaluation shows it
improves throughput by up to 2.94× and reduces latency by
up to 85.2%, compared with the state-of-the-art systems.
